content.text: Lighthouses have guided sailors for thousands of years, and their purpose has barely changed even as their technology has transformed. Early examples were simple fires kindled on high ground or towers, such as the ancient Pharos of Alexandria, which was counted among the wonders of the world. Over time, builders learned to pair towers with powerful lamps and carefully shaped lenses. The Fresnel lens, developed in the early nineteenth century, could throw a beam many miles across the water using a ring of glass prisms instead of heavy, costly mirrors. Each lighthouse was given its own signature, a pattern of flashes and colors, so that a navigator could tell one from another on a chart at night. Today most stations run on electricity and automated sensors, and many have been abandoned as satellite navigation took over. Even so, lighthouses remain landmarks of hope and steadiness. Many have become museums or guesthouses, and people still climb their spiral stairs to see the coastline spread out below. They stand as reminders that a single steady light, placed in the right spot, can keep ships away from danger.
